feedback: When the heading matches the dance angle and the set distance matches the waggle duration: 'You landed on the flowers — you read both parts of the code.'
When the direction is right but distance is wrong: 'Right way, wrong distance — the LENGTH of each waggle run tells you how far, not just the angle.'
When the angle is misread: 'You went the wrong way — the ANGLE of the straight waggle run from straight up on the comb is the angle to fly measured from the sun's direction.'
When producing the dance: 'Check both variables — does your dance angle point toward the patch, and does your waggle length match how far it is?'
activities.intendedInsight: The little dance is a real message that carries TWO pieces of information at once — which direction and how far — a decodable code, not just excited wiggling. Producing the dance as well as reading it shows the code works from both ends.
learnerActions: Watch a forager bee perform a waggle dance: a straight 'waggle run' tilted at an angle, then a loop back, repeated over and over.

Read the two pieces of information: use the ANGLE of the straight run from straight up on the comb to work out the direction to the flowers (that same angle measured from the sun's direction), and use how LONG each waggle run lasts to judge the distance.
Set your heading at the dance's angle measured from the sun's direction and set a distance from the waggle duration, then 'fly out' to try to reach the flower patch.
If you overshoot, fall short, or head the wrong way, watch the bee dance again and adjust your reading.
Then swap roles: given a flower patch in a chosen position, perform the correct dance (right angle, right waggle length) so hive-mates could find it.
activities.title: Decode and perform the waggle dance

feedback: If a learner treats the trail as permanent: 'Watch again with no ants using it — the trail fades. It only stays while ants keep reinforcing it.'
If a learner says it is not communication because there are no words: 'The chemical IS the message — it changes where other ants go, so it carries information.'
activities.intendedInsight: A pheromone trail is a chemical message: it carries 'food this way', builds up when reinforced by traffic, and evaporates when not — so it is a signal, not a fixed path.
learnerActions: Draw a scent (pheromone) trail between the nest and a food source.
Watch what happens as more ants travel the trail — notice it strengthens with traffic.
Stop the traffic and observe the trail fade over time.
Explain in your own words why a trail is NOT a permanent road and what information it carries to other ants.
activities.title: Lay an ant trail that strengthens and fades

feedback: If a learner assumes all fireflies flash the same: 'Compare two patterns — the timing differs. The pattern is a code that usually identifies the species.'
If the pattern is reproduced incorrectly: 'Check the timing and order of the flashes — that sequence is what carries the message.'
activities.intendedInsight: Flashes are species-specific codes — a signal using light. Different species use different patterns, so the pattern itself carries meaning to the right receiver.
learnerActions: Observe different firefly flash patterns (timing and sequence of flashes).
Reproduce a given species' flash pattern.
Match a flash pattern to the species that uses it, and explain who the signal is for and why (finding a mate).
activities.title: Match firefly flash patterns to species

feedback: If a learner says one butterfly makes the whole round-trip: 'The journey spans several generations — different butterflies complete different legs.'
If a learner calls migration a form of communication: 'Ask: is one monarch sending a signal to change another's behaviour? Migration is travelling and navigating, not signalling.'
activities.intendedInsight: Migration is a remarkable navigational behaviour, but it is NOT communication — it does not pass information to another insect to change its behaviour. This contrast sharpens the definition of communication.
learnerActions: Trace the monarch butterfly migration across a continent-spanning map, following the route over thousands of kilometres.
Describe what makes the journey remarkable in terms of distance and navigation.
Note that the full round-trip spans multiple generations — one butterfly does not complete it alone.
Decide and justify: is migrating the same as communicating, or is it something different?
activities.title: Navigate the monarch migration — and ask: is this communication?

feedback: If a learner says the bee is just excited/random: 'Move the food and the dance angle and length change with it — a meaning that reliably maps to location is information, not excitement.'

If a learner says the bee flies off and the others just follow behind: 'The other bees read the dance INSIDE the hive, then fly out on their own. The information is transmitted, not demonstrated by leading — telling where is different from guiding there.'

If a learner says insects can't communicate because they can't talk: 'Communication is any signal carrying information — chemical trails, light flashes, chirps, and the dance all change another insect's behaviour without words.'
activities.intendedInsight: Communication is a signal that carries information and changes another animal's behaviour. The dance is not mere excitement: the angle encodes direction and the waggle duration encodes distance, and hive-mates decode it inside the hive before flying out on their own.
learnerActions: Consider the claim: 'When a honeybee finds flowers, it just gets excited and wiggles about.' Decide whether that is right.
Explain what the waggle dance actually does, what information it carries, and why that counts as communication.
Answer a follow-up: HOW does one dance show BOTH direction AND distance — what part of the dance carries each?
Explain whether an ant's chemical trail and a firefly's flash also count as communication, and why.
activities.title: Explain what the waggle dance does (diagnostic discussion)
